thoughts: Russian «а» is basically an “ah” vowel when stressed, but it often reduces (sounds more like a short, centralized “uh”) when unstressed. The main challenge for English speakers is remembering that vowel quality depends heavily on stress, not spelling.
description: Pronounce «а» as an open “ah” sound when stressed (close to the vowel in English “father,” but usually shorter and cleaner). When «а» is unstressed, it commonly reduces toward a more relaxed sound like “uh” (as in the first syllable of “about,” but a bit more open). Don’t turn it into the English “a” in “cat” (/æ/).

thoughts: Russian «б» is basically the English B sound, but learners must watch for (1) a “soft” palatalized version before soft vowels/ь and (2) devoicing to [p] at the end of words or before voiceless consonants.
description: «б» is a voiced bilabial stop [b], like English b in “bat.” Before «е, ё, и, ю, я» or «ь», it becomes “soft” [bʲ]: make a normal B, but add a slight “y” quality by raising the tongue toward the hard palate (similar to starting to say “by-”). At the end of a word (and often before a voiceless consonant), «б» is devoiced and sounds like [p], though it is still spelled «б».

thoughts: Russian «в» is basically the English V sound, but it often changes: it becomes devoiced to an F-like sound at the end of a word or before a voiceless consonant, and it becomes “soft” (slightly y‑colored) before front vowels or ь.
description:
Main sound: like English **v** in *voice* (upper teeth on lower lip; don’t make it a **w**). 
Common changes: 
- **Devoicing**: at the **end of a word** or before a **voiceless consonant** (п, ф, к, т, с, ш, х, ц, ч), «в» is pronounced closer to **f**. 
- **Soft (palatalized) в**: before **е/ё/и/ю/я** or **ь**, it’s a “softer” **v** (/vʲ/), like a **v** with a slight **y** glide.

thoughts: Pattern: «г». For English speakers it’s basically the normal hard G sound, but Russian adds (1) a “soft” palatalized version before front vowels and (2) regular final/assimilation devoicing, so «г» can sound like K at the end of a word or before voiceless consonants.
description: Usually pronounced like English /g/ in “go” (a voiced hard G). Before front vowels (е, ё, и, ю, я) it becomes “soft” [gʲ]—like a G with a slight ‘y’ color. At the end of a word (or before a voiceless consonant), it devoices to [k], so it may sound like K (e.g., final «-г»).

thoughts: Russian «д» is basically an English D, but it’s typically more dental (tongue closer to the upper teeth). Watch for the soft (palatalized) version before «е/ё/и/ю/я/ь», and for final devoicing: «д» at the end of a word is pronounced like «т».
description: «д» is a voiced stop like English “d” (as in “dog”), usually made with the tongue touching the upper teeth/teeth ridge (more dental than many English Ds). Before «е, ё, и, ю, я» or «ь» it becomes “soft” (palatalized) [dʲ], sounding like a D with a slight “y” coloring. At the end of a word, «д» is devoiced and sounds like [t].

thoughts: Russian «е» has a “ye/eh” quality. English speakers usually recognize the basic sound (like ‘yes’ / ‘met’), but the tricky part is that «е» often makes the previous consonant soft (palatalized), and when unstressed it can reduce toward an ‘ih’ sound.
description: Main pronunciations: (1) At the beginning of a word (or after a vowel / «ь» / «ъ»), «е» is like “ye” [je] (similar to the start of English “yes”). (2) After a consonant, it’s closer to “e” as in “met” [e], but it also softens (palatalizes) the previous consonant—so it’s not just a plain English ‘e’. (3) When unstressed, «е» is often reduced toward an ‘ih’ sound [ɪ].

thoughts: Russian «ё» is essentially a stressed “yo” sound. English speakers usually recognize it from transliterations like -yov/-yov (e.g., Gorbachyov/Gorbachev), but the tricky part is that after a consonant it also makes that consonant “soft” (palatalized). Also, in Russian print it’s often written as «е» even when pronounced «ё».
description: «ё» is pronounced like English “yo” in “yoga” (/jo/). At the beginning of a word or after a vowel/«ь»/«ъ», you clearly hear the “y” glide: /jo/. After a consonant, it’s usually /ʲo/: the consonant becomes soft (your tongue rises toward the hard palate) and then you say “o”—often without a strong separate “y” sound.

thoughts: Russian «ж» is the voiced partner of «ш». English speakers often map it to the “zh” sound in *measure*, but Russian usually has a slightly “darker,” more retracted sound, and it devoices at the end of a word or before voiceless consonants.
description: Pronounce «ж» as a voiced “zh” sound (like the middle of *mea*s*ure*), but typically with the tongue a bit farther back and with some lip rounding. Tip: start from Russian/English-like “sh” and add voicing (make your throat vibrate). In Russian it becomes devoiced (sounds like «ш») at the end of a word or before a voiceless consonant.

thoughts: Russian «з» is basically the voiced “z” sound. The main surprises for English speakers are (1) final devoicing (it becomes like “s” at the end of a word) and (2) softening/palatalization before «е, ё, и, ю, я» or «ь», giving a slightly “y”-colored z.
description: Pronounce «з» like English **z** in “zoo” (a voiced buzzing sound). In Russian it often **devoices** to **[s]** at the **end of a word** or before a voiceless consonant (so written «з» may sound like “s”). Before «е, ё, и, ю, я» or «ь», it becomes **soft** («зь»), like a slightly “y”-tinged z (keep the tongue closer to the hard palate).

thoughts: Russian «и» is basically the /i/ (“ee”) vowel, but it’s typically shorter/tenser than in English and it usually makes the previous consonant “soft” (palatalized). After «ж/ш/ц» it’s pronounced noticeably closer to Russian «ы» (more like [ɨ] than [i]).
description: Pronounce «и» like the vowel in English “see” (/i/), but keep it pure (no glide) and fairly short. A key difference: before «и», most Russian consonants become “soft” (your tongue rises toward the hard palate, kind of a subtle “y” color). Special case: after «ж», «ш», and «ц», «и» is usually more central, closer to [ɨ] (similar in feel to Russian «ы», not a clear “ee”).

thoughts: The Russian letter «й» (called “short i”) is the consonant glide /j/, very close to English Y. The main pitfall for English speakers is turning it into a full vowel like “ee” instead of a quick glide.

thoughts: Pattern: «к». It’s the Russian letter for a /k/ sound. English speakers know /k/, but Russian «к» is typically less aspirated (less of a puff of air), and it has a soft (palatalized) version before front vowels like «и/е».
description: «к» is a voiceless velar stop, like the K in English “skate” (a clean, unaspirated /k/). Before front vowels (especially «и», also «е/ё/ю/я») it becomes “soft” (palatalized), roughly like trying to say /k/ while your tongue is moving toward a “y” sound: [kʲ]. Tip: avoid the strong English puff of air you hear in “kite”; aim for the tighter K in “skate.”

thoughts: Russian «л» is an L sound, but it has two main versions: a hard/dark [ɫ] (often darker than English) and a soft/palatalized [lʲ] (like adding a small “y” quality). English speakers know an L sound already, but the soft vs hard contrast takes practice.
description: Pronounce «л» with the tongue tip against the ridge just behind the upper front teeth. In many contexts it’s a hard/dark L [ɫ] (similar to the “l” in English “full,” often even darker). Before «е, ё, и, ю, я» or with «ь», it becomes soft «ль» [lʲ]: keep the tongue in L position but also raise the middle of the tongue toward the hard palate—like the “lli” sound in English “million.”

thoughts: «м» is essentially the same sound as English M, with an additional common Russian ‘soft’ (palatalized) version before front vowels (е/ё/и/ю/я) or ь.

thoughts: The letter «н» represents the Russian N sound. English speakers already know the basic sound [n], but Russian also has a very common “soft” (palatalized) version «нь / н» before certain vowels, which can sound like an N with a subtle “y” color.
description: «н» is usually like English **n** in *no* (a voiced alveolar nasal). In many positions Russian also has a **soft (palatalized) н [nʲ]**—most often before **е, ё, и, ю, я** or with **ь**—where the middle of your tongue lifts toward the hard palate, giving a slight “ny” quality (like the *ny* in *canyon*, but without adding an extra vowel). In fast speech, «н» may also assimilate to neighboring consonants (e.g., sound more like **m** before **б/п/м/ф/в**, or more “ng”-like before **к/г/х**), but a clear [n] is always understood.

thoughts: Russian «о» is straightforward when stressed (a pure, rounded [o]), but it changes noticeably when unstressed (often reduced toward [a]/[ə] in most standard accents). English speakers usually know the basic vowel quality but not the systematic reduction.
description: Stressed «о» is a pure, rounded vowel [o] (similar to the vowel in British English “thought,” but keep it steady—don’t glide into an “oh” diphthong). Unstressed «о» is typically reduced: often closer to [a] (especially right before the stress) or to a more neutral [ə] in other unstressed positions (this is the common ‘akanye’ pattern).

thoughts: Russian «п» is basically an English P sound, but typically with much less aspiration (less “puff of air”). It also has a common “soft” (palatalized) version before «е, ё, и, ю, я» or «ь», which can be new for English speakers.
description: «п» is a voiceless bilabial stop: close both lips and release, like English “p” in “spin” (unaspirated). At the start of a stressed syllable, avoid the strong English-style burst of air (don’t make it sound like “ph”). Before «е, ё, и, ю, я» or «ь», it’s usually “soft” «пь» [pʲ]: say the P while raising the middle of your tongue toward the hard palate—similar to the start of “pew,” but as one consonant.

thoughts: Russian «р» is a rolled/tapped R (not the English R). It has a hard version [r] and a palatalized (“soft”) version [rʲ] before «е ё и ю я» or «ь». Many English speakers recognize the idea from Spanish/Italian, but producing a clear trill and the soft [rʲ] contrast can take practice.
description: Pronounce «р» with the tip of your tongue at the alveolar ridge (just behind your upper teeth), vibrating (a trill) or at least tapping quickly. It is not the English /ɹ/ (which is smooth and pulled back). Before «е ё и ю я» or «ь», it becomes “soft” [rʲ]: keep the trill/tap, but also raise the middle of the tongue toward the hard palate (like adding a light ‘y’ flavor). Practice tip: start with a single quick tap (like the Spanish single-r in ‘pero’) and build to a trill; keep airflow steady and tongue relaxed.

thoughts: Russian «с» is basically the English S sound, but it can become voiced (like Z) before a voiced consonant, and it can be “soft” (palatalized) before certain vowels/ь.

Before soft vowels (е, ё, и, ю, я) or «ь», it becomes “soft” [sʲ]—like an /s/ with a subtle “y” glide toward “sh” but not actually “sh”.

thoughts: Russian «т» is a voiceless T-like stop. The main pitfalls for English speakers are (1) keeping it unaspirated (no strong puff of air) and (2) making it “soft” (palatalized) before letters like е/и/я/ю/ё or ь.
description: «т» is usually like English “t” in “stop” (a crisp, unaspirated [t], with the tongue against the teeth/alveolar ridge). Before “soft” contexts (е, ё, и, ю, я, ь) it becomes palatalized [tʲ], sounding a bit like a “t” plus a subtle “y” coloring. Avoid the strong English aspirated “t” (like in “top”).

thoughts: Russian «у» is essentially the /u/ vowel (like “oo”), with noticeable reduction to a shorter, more relaxed sound when unstressed. The main trap for English speakers is avoiding a preceding “y” glide (*/ju/*).

Before е/и it can sound slightly “softer” (more forward).

thoughts: The Russian hard sign (ъ) is not a vowel or consonant sound by itself. It’s a spelling/phonetic marker that forces a clear break: the consonant before it stays “hard” (non-palatalized), and the following vowel (е/ё/ю/я) starts with a distinct English-like “y” glide [j].
description: ъ is silent, but it changes how you pronounce the letters around it. After a consonant + ъ + е/ё/ю/я, say a clear “y” sound before the vowel (like the start of “yes”), and do NOT soften (palatalize) the consonant before ъ. Roughly: Cъе/ё/ю/я ≈ C + “y” + vowel (e.g., объект ≈ ab-YEKT).

thoughts: Russian «ы» is a distinct vowel (roughly [ɨ]) that English doesn’t have as a separate phoneme. It often feels like trying to say “ih/ee” while pulling the tongue farther back; keeping the lips unrounded is key. English speakers usually confuse it with «и» at first.
description: Pronounce «ы» as a close-to-mid, back-ish, unrounded vowel (IPA: [ɨ]). It’s not the English “ee” (as in *see*) and not the English “uh” (as in *but*), but somewhere between: start near “ih” (*bit*), then pull the tongue back (toward where it is for “uh”) while keeping it relatively high, and keep lips relaxed/unrounded. A practical trick: say “ee” and, without changing your lip shape, retract the tongue slightly; the sound should get darker and less “smiley” than «и».

thoughts: Ь (the soft sign) isn’t a vowel sound on its own. It mainly tells you to make the previous consonant “soft” (palatalized), and before я/ю/ё/е it also signals a little /y/ glide (like starting the vowel with a quick “y”). English doesn’t use this as a regular, meaning-changing feature, so learners often either ignore it or add an extra vowel.
description: Pronounce ь by modifying the consonant before it: make that consonant “soft” by raising the middle of your tongue toward the hard palate, often sounding like a very light added “y” quality (but without inserting a separate vowel). At the end of a word, it simply means the final consonant is soft. Before я/ю/ё/е (e.g., -ья-, -ью-), it both softens the consonant and makes the following vowel start with a /y/ glide: -ья- ≈ “-yа-”, -ью- ≈ “-yu-”.

Before a voiceless consonant or at word end, it can devoice toward /t͡s/ (similar to «ц»).

thoughts: The letter pattern "сч" is almost always pronounced as one merged sound, the same as the single Russian letter "щ": a long, very soft/palatal “sh”-like sound. English speakers often try to say it as separate “s” + “ch,” which usually sounds accented in Russian.
description: In most words, "сч" is pronounced like "щ": a long, soft hissy sound [ɕː] (often written “shch” in transliteration, but it’s essentially one prolonged sound). Aim for an English “sh,” but with the tongue higher and more forward (closer to the hard palate) and hold it a little longer. Only in very careful/slow enunciation might you hear it as two parts (“s” + “ch”), but that’s not the normal everyday pronunciation.

thoughts: In modern Russian spelling, the letter sequence "зч" is quite rare because prefixes usually switch to "с" before "ч" (so you more often see "сч"). When it does occur (often in older/archaic spelling), it’s pronounced the same way as "сч": essentially like "щ"—a long, soft (palatalized) "shch" sound.
description: Pronounce "зч" with regressive assimilation: the "з" devoices and merges with "ч", giving a sound like Russian "щ"—roughly a long, soft "shch" ([ɕː] or [ɕt͡ɕ]). For English speakers, think of saying “fresh cheese” quickly so “sh + ch” run together, but in Russian it’s softer (tongue closer to the hard palate) and often lengthened.

thoughts: The letter sequence «жч» is normally not pronounced as separate sounds. In most natural speech it assimilates and merges into a single long, soft “shch”-like sound (similar to «щ»). English speakers usually need to focus on (1) making it softer (more like the “sh” in “she”) and (2) holding it slightly longer.
description: In standard modern Russian, «жч» is usually pronounced as a single long soft hushing sound [ɕː]—very close to «щ». It’s like saying a very soft “sh” (as in English “she”), but with the tongue a bit higher/closer to the hard palate, and held longer (almost like “shsh” compressed into one sound). In very careful, spelling-based pronunciation you may occasionally hear something closer to [ʐt͡ɕ] (“zh” + “ch”), but the normal target is the merged [ɕː].

thoughts: In Russian, the letter cluster «дч» is usually not pronounced as a clear /d/ + /ch/. The /d/ assimilates (devoices) and effectively merges with «ч», so you get a single long, soft “ch” sound. English speakers know “ch”, but the Russian «ч» is more palatal (softer) and the slight lengthening can be unfamiliar.
description: Most commonly «дч» is pronounced as a long soft «ч»: roughly [t͡ɕː] (often like “чч” in sound). Don’t try to voice a /d/ before it—let the «д» devoice and merge into the «ч». In faster speech the length may reduce, sounding closer to a normal single Russian «ч» [t͡ɕ]. Tip: say Russian «ч» (like English “ch” in *chew* but noticeably softer/palatal), and hold it just a touch longer.

description: Most often «зж» is pronounced as a single long Russian «ж» sound: [ʐː] (like the ‘zh’ in English “measure,” but usually darker/farther back, and held longer). Tip: keep voicing on the whole time and don’t insert a vowel between the consonants—just “hold” the zh/friction a little longer.

Think of English “hearts” /harts/: the Russian cluster is similar, but with Russian tapped/rolled «р» and a single, clean «ц» (ts), not an extra syllable.

In very careful, slow speech you may sometimes hear all consonants [lnts], but dropping «л» is the standard, natural outcome in everyday speech.

thoughts: The soft sign (ь) is not a vowel and has no sound by itself. At the end of a word it mainly tells you to pronounce the previous consonant “soft” (palatalized), which is a key Russian feature that English spelling doesn’t mark.
description: Ь (the “soft sign”) is **not pronounced on its own**. When it appears **at the end of a word**, it means the **preceding consonant is “soft” (palatalized)**: say the consonant while raising the middle of your tongue toward the hard palate, as if adding a very slight **‘y’ quality**—but **without adding a separate ‘ee/yuh’ vowel**. For example, final **-ль** can sound a bit like the softened “l” in *million*; final **-рь** is like an r with a light ‘y’ coloring (many learners approximate it as “ry” at first, but keep it tight—no extra syllable).
